title: Traditional game design may not work for generative AI games
author: upforest
selftext:
**I don’t think traditional game design principles are suitable for generative AI games. We’re no longer just designing game mechanics, instead we’re designing the mechanics that generate game mechanics. As I see it, GenAI games are a new art form.**

Traditionally, game designers create the mechanics: the rules, progression systems, combat, quests, interactions, rewards, and boundaries of the world. Players explore a possibility space that was largely designed in advance.  
But with generative AI, I think we’re moving one level higher.

We’re no longer just designing game mechanics. We’re designing the mechanics that generate game mechanics.  
Instead of deciding exactly what a character will say, we design the personality, memory, motivations, relationships, and constraints that determine how that character behaves.

Instead of writing every quest, we design systems capable of creating situations, conflicts, goals, and stories dynamically.

Instead of designing every possible interaction between players and the world, we design the underlying rules that allow new interactions to emerge.

That changes the role of the game designer.

The designer becomes less like someone constructing a fixed playground and more like someone designing a generative ecosystem, a set of rules, agents, and feedback loops capable of continuously producing new gameplay.

Whether people agree or not, we need a new game design discipline focused not on designing experiences directly, but on designing systems capable of creating experiences themselves.

comments.author: RickRelentless
comments.body: Are you not describing the difference between a game designer and a game director, as it already exists in ‘traditional’ game dev?

replies.author: upforest
replies.body: This is interesting. Just like coders aren’t really coding anymore, but they’re still coders, doing what their managers tell them to do.

replies.author: mccoypauley
replies.body:
I think there’s a distinction between engineering and development. As a software developer, I spend very little time sitting down and writing code these days because of AI, but it’s always been the case that we do planning “about” what we’re going to produce. That’s the engineering part.

Although your larger point—that we’re now designing towards probabilistic behavior—is a genuine shift. I think while the same engineering principles in game design apply, for some games where it’s more like setting up an unpredictable aquarium for players to be immersed in, it’s a different paradigm when it comes to engineering.

replies.author: Spytle
replies.body:
yes, exactly.

And as for the mechanics themselves, this is a debatable "level up" because it really depends on the results.

Running with this scenario of it creatign a Game Director role, I do not use the tools to rethink the rules of game design, or even how I develop mecahanics, I use them to get my brush closer to the canvas.

comments.author: Jolva
comments.body: Neat thought experiment but I don't have characters or relationships in my game. Using human language to describe how you want the world to react was always the starting point in game development I think. Prior to large language models you'd build all of the systems you describe by hand. Making that process easier is the only thing that's different.

replies.author: upforest
replies.body: I think the difference goes beyond making development easier. Traditionally, we build the systems ourselves. With GenAI, we build systems that can generate new systems, behaviors, or mechanics at runtime. Before GenAI, studios made games as products. With GenAI, studios can make “studios” as the product.

replies.author: bettertagsweretaken
replies.body: This is what kills me with the anti crowd. Like, don't you just want to be able to wave your hand and conjure a fun game? Wouldn't that be cool? Why do people want it to be a difficult, laborious process for artists and programmers to accomplish what they want?

replies.author: upforest
replies.body: Agreed. I guess those who oppose GenAI games today would have opposed electronic games back in the 1970s while happily playing board games.

comments.author: Open_Organization997
comments.body: If you're not doing the GD of your game yourself it has 99.9% chance of being bad or just a sad copy.

comments.author: YKLKTMA
comments.body:
This is complete nonsense. The principles of game design do not change as long as games are made for humans.

You should at least learn the fundamentals before broadcasting your "smart" opinions

replies.author: upforest
replies.body:
People love drawing, but that didn’t stop photography from thriving. And photography went on to develop its own artistic principles and techniques. 

May I ask you a question? Would you rather have a painter paint your portrait, or just take a photo with your phone?

replies.author: YKLKTMA
replies.body:
You are confusing new tools and production techniques with fundamental design principles. Photography didn't make composition or human visual perception obsolete, and AI tools don't make game design principles obsolete. Like a generated quest still needs clear goals, meaningful choices, proper pacing, feedback, and balance, nothing changed.   
Your portrait question is irrelevant because different tools serve different purposes.  
Learn the basics first; don't spit nonsense

replies.author: upforest
replies.body:
I didn’t say AI makes game design obsolete. Even sculpture still exists.

But I do bet GenAI games will gradually come to dominate the market.

replies.author: YKLKTMA
replies.body:
That has nothing to do with your original claim.

You said traditional game design principles are unsuitable for GenAI games. Whether GenAI games eventually dominate the market doesn't support that statement in any way.

You are repeatedly confusing market adoption and production technology with fundamental design principles. Stop betting on things you don't understand

replies.author: upforest
replies.body:
You are missing some basic common sense that I thought you already understood.

GenAI game design is a superset of traditional game design. In my experience, not everyone knows how to design GenAI systems properly. It is agreed that game design takes some talent to master, and the same is true for GenAI system design.

replies.author: YKLKTMA
replies.body:
You have now argued yourself into my position.

If GenAI game design is a superset of traditional game design, then traditional game design principles are not unsuitable - they are a necessary subset of it.

Saying that GenAI systems require additional expertise is obvious, but it is also completely different from your original claim.

As for your point that not everyone knows how to design GenAI systems properly: not everyone, including you, seems to understand what design is in general, or what game design is in particular.

comments.author: CubeUnleashed
comments.body: You're right with the part about designing the mechanics that generate game mechanics. I'm releasing a hidden objects game in November and AI built a system where I can place objects on designated backgrounds and assign them functions.

comments.author: Nasilbitatbirakti
comments.body: Am I the only one who's underwhelmed by AI? It's been years and where are the results of these so called miracle tools? With AI I'm wasting days to even prototype a basic concept which is not extremely broken and it's always bloated and not working as intended anyway. I end up doing everything manually with a little guidance from AI here and there.

replies.author: re-skob
replies.body:
there are large differences between the cheap or free AI and the AI that costs the subscription fee. If you're underwhelmed by AI then you probably haven't paid the subscription fee and you haven't paid it because you're underwhelmed and don't have a good reason to pay it. It's a pretty funny feedback loop. So no, you're not the only one underwhelmed by AI, but you're also likely not using the best of it. I could spin up a full game in a couple of hours without touching a single line of code.

And you're seeing the results everywhere, you just don't know they're the results because they're not advertised to you as the results of it - the majority of devs are just using it and doing their work behind the scenes using AI. A lot of the speed increase is still bogged down by the processes that have developed at large organizations so maybe things come out 1.5x - 2x faster instead of 10x or 100x but it's not like you're privy to the schedules they would be under if they weren't using AI.

comments.author: robobax
comments.body: You are literally describing game design at the high level.

comments.author: imnotabot303
comments.body:
Sounds like a bunch of hogwash to me. All that AI is doing for most people is letting them jump into making a game with zero skills, zero experience and only a vague idea of what they want to achieve. Even then what they want to achieve is usually just a worse AI version of something that already exists.

A dev with some knowledge and experience will be using AI in a completely different way than someone who doesn't have any. Game devs will use it as a tool, non game devs will use it as a crutch.

It's the same with all AI. With AI art for example, no artist wants to just type some words to make an image, they will use it as part of the process so it becomes a tool not a magic button.

replies.author: Benhamish-WH-Allen
replies.body:
I’d probably write something like this:  
I think you’re identifying a genuine shift, but I’d take it one step further.  
Traditional games are largely about designing mechanics. Generative games are about designing systems that generate mechanics. But the next frontier may be designing **judgment**.  
Instead of asking, “What content should the player experience?” we’re asking, “What principles should this world use to create, evaluate, and respond to experiences?”  
That means designing memory, priorities, uncertainty, trade-offs, and consequences—not just content generators. The most interesting AI characters won’t be the ones that can say anything; they’ll be the ones that consistently decide *why* they say something, when they choose not to act, and how previous experiences change future decisions.  
Likewise, endless procedural content isn’t necessarily compelling. Meaning comes from persistence: actions that matter, worlds that remember, and systems that evolve because of what has happened rather than simply producing endless novelty.  
It feels less like designing a game and more like designing a society with its own values, institutions, and feedback loops. The gameplay then emerges from the interaction between the player and that living system, rather than from handcrafted sequences of content.  
I think that reframes the discussion from “AI can generate infinite quests” to “AI can embody a coherent way of making decisions,” which is a much more interesting design problem.

replies.author: upforest
replies.body: Wait a second. I don't think you get the point. Nobody is saying GenAI game development is for people with zero skills. In fact, it can require even more knowledge than traditional game design. You need to understand GenAI engineering as well as game design. The point is that game designers who don’t know how to design GenAI systems are the ones who will gradually fall behind.

replies.author: imnotabot303
replies.body:
You absolutely do not need to know "AI engineering" whatever that is, to use AI to make games.

All the things you describe are things normal to game dev.

Let's take your character example. If you're creating a character for a story driven game you would think about all those things anyway. A background for you character, a personality type, their likes or dislikes etc. That's just how you create a believable character and dialogue. If you're suggesting people will just make a list of characters traits and a plot and then give it to an LLM to generate dialogue then you're likely going to end up with slop.
